title: Ezekiel 11:1–13
context: Ezekiel continues to narrate his vision of Jerusalem (chapters 8–11). The Spirit brings him to the east gate of the LORD’s house, where twenty-five leaders are giving wicked counsel. They say, “This is the cauldron, and we are the meat,” apparently claiming that the city’s walls will protect them as a pot protects meat. The LORD tells Ezekiel to prophesy against them: only the slain will remain in the city, while the leaders will be brought out and judged at the border of Israel. As Ezekiel prophesies, Pelatiah son of Benaiah dies, and Ezekiel falls on his face and cries out for the remnant. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about false security and God’s judgment on unjust leaders.

verses.text: Moreover the Spirit lifted me up and brought me to the east gate of the LORD’s house, which looks eastward. Behold, twenty-five men were at the door of the gate; and I saw among them Jaazaniah the son of Azzur, and Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, princes of the people.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ezekiel reports that the Spirit brought him to the east gate of the LORD’s house, where he saw twenty-five men, including Jaazaniah son of Azzur and Pelatiah son of Benaiah, princes of the people.

Arminian readers see leaders held responsible for the counsel they give.
verses.reformedNotes:
This is still part of the vision that began in chapter 8. This Jaazaniah is distinguished by his father’s name from the Jaazaniah son of Shaphan in 8:11.

Reformed readers see God exposing hidden leadership. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: He said to me, “Son of man, these are the men who devise iniquity, and who give wicked counsel in this city;
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD tells Ezekiel that these men devise iniquity and give wicked counsel in the city. The leaders are named as the source of the trouble.

Arminian readers see responsibility resting on those who shape a people’s choices.
verses.reformedNotes:
The prophet is addressed as “Son of man,” the title used throughout Ezekiel for the human messenger.

Reformed readers see God knowing and judging the counsel of rulers. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the accountability of leaders for the advice they give.

verses.text: who say, ‘The time is not near to build houses. This is the cauldron, and we are the meat.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The leaders say, “This is the cauldron, and we are the meat.” Their saying claims safety inside Jerusalem’s walls, as meat is protected in a pot.

Arminian readers see false confidence encouraging the city to ignore the warnings.
verses.reformedNotes:
The first clause, about building houses, is difficult; it may dismiss the need for long-term planning or mock warnings of exile. The cauldron image returns in 24:3–6.

Reformed readers see pride resting on the wrong security. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Therefore prophesy against them. Prophesy, son of man.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD commands Ezekiel twice to prophesy against these men. The repetition adds urgency.

Arminian readers see the prophet sent to confront leaders whose counsel was misleading the city, so that the people might still hear the truth.
verses.reformedNotes:
The double command, “Prophesy, son of man,” stresses that the word must be spoken.

Reformed readers see God’s word sent against those who resist it. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the prophet’s calling to speak God’s word whether or not it is welcome.

verses.text: The LORD’s Spirit fell on me, and he said to me, “Speak, ‘The LORD says: “Thus you have said, house of Israel; for I know the things that come into your mind.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s Spirit falls on Ezekiel, and the LORD says he knows what comes into the minds of the house of Israel. Nothing is hidden from him.

Arminian readers see God’s knowledge of hearts as the basis for a just response to what people truly intend.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse highlights God’s knowledge of thoughts as well as words.

Reformed readers see God’s full knowledge of the heart. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the reach of God’s knowledge, which no human counsel can escape or conceal.

verses.text: You have multiplied your slain in this city, and you have filled its streets with the slain.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says they have multiplied the slain in the city and filled its streets with them. The leaders’ counsel has cost lives.

Arminian readers see the leaders held responsible for violence their policies produced, whether directly or by injustice.
verses.reformedNotes:
The text does not specify whether this refers to judicial killings, oppression, or deaths caused by disastrous policy; readers differ.

Reformed readers see bloodshed as a mark of the city’s guilt. Both traditions read this as shared ground and keep the meaning hedged.

verses.text: “ ‘Therefore the Lord GOD says: “Your slain whom you have laid in the middle of it, they are the meat, and this is the cauldron; but you will be brought out of the middle of it.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord GOD turns the saying around: the slain are the meat and the city is the cauldron, but the leaders will be brought out. Their image is reversed.

Arminian readers see their false security undone by their own words.
verses.reformedNotes:
In the leaders’ saying the pot protected them; in the LORD’s answer only the dead remain in it, and the living leaders will be taken out to judgment.

Reformed readers see God overturning human boasts. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: You have feared the sword; and I will bring the sword on you,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says they feared the sword, and he will bring the sword on them. What they feared will come.

Arminian readers see the consequences of trusting in walls rather than in obedience to God, which the leaders refused.
verses.reformedNotes:
The pattern of feared disaster arriving anyway recurs in the prophets (compare Jeremiah 42:16).

Reformed readers see God’s judgment matching the sin. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the futility of seeking security apart from God.

verses.text: “I will bring you out of the middle of it, and deliver you into the hands of strangers, and will execute judgments among you.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will bring them out of the city and hand them to strangers, executing judgments among them. Removal from the city is itself judgment.

Arminian readers see judgment following persistent refusal of the prophets’ warnings.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse anticipates exile and defeat at the hands of foreign powers.

Reformed readers see God working judgment through the nations. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s rule over history and the reality of judgment on the city’s leaders.

verses.text: You will fall by the sword. I will judge you in the border of Israel. Then you will know that I am the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
They will fall by the sword and be judged at the border of Israel, and then they will know that the LORD is God. Judgment brings recognition.

Arminian readers see judgment as revealing God’s identity.
verses.reformedNotes:
Many readers connect judgment “in the border of Israel” with the judgment at Riblah after Jerusalem fell (2 Kings 25:6), though the text does not name the place.

Reformed readers see God vindicating his name. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: This will not be your cauldron, neither will you be the meat in the middle of it. I will judge you in the border of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
The city will not be their cauldron, nor they the meat within it; they will be judged at Israel’s border. The saying is finally rejected.

Arminian readers see the leaders denied the safety they claimed for themselves.
verses.reformedNotes:
The repeated reference to the border reinforces the reversal of verse 3.

Reformed readers see God’s word overruling human claims. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the emptiness of false security and the certainty of God’s word.

verses.text: You will know that I am the LORD, for you have not walked in my statutes. You have not executed my ordinances, but have done after the ordinances of the nations that are around you.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
They will know the LORD, for they did not walk in his statutes but followed the ordinances of the surrounding nations. The cause is named.

Arminian readers see covenant unfaithfulness chosen in imitation of the nations.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse connects judgment with abandoning God’s law for other customs.

Reformed readers see the covenant broken by conformity to the nations. Both traditions read this as shared ground about faithfulness to God’s ways rather than the ways of surrounding peoples.

verses.text: When I prophesied, Pelatiah the son of Benaiah died. Then I fell down on my face, and cried with a loud voice, and said, “Ah Lord GOD! Will you make a full end of the remnant of Israel?”
verses.arminianNotes:
As Ezekiel prophesies, Pelatiah son of Benaiah dies. Ezekiel falls on his face and cries, “Ah Lord GOD! Will you make a full end of the remnant of Israel?”

Arminian readers see the prophet interceding in anguish.
verses.reformedNotes:
The cry closely resembles Ezekiel’s plea in 9:8. The text does not explain the manner of Pelatiah’s death.

Reformed readers see a prophet who grieves over judgment. Both traditions read this as shared ground about compassion in the face of God’s judgment.
